Dear Nazia didi,

You asked why I picked commerce when I've always loved biology. I've been avoiding the answer, but here it is.

When the stream forms came, all five of my friends ticked commerce. Every single one. In the group chat they kept saying, "Commerce gang!" and making plans to sit together in Class 11.

I sat with the form for an hour. My hand kept going to biology. But then I pictured walking into a class where I knew nobody, and my stomach went tight. I didn't want to be the odd one out.

So I ticked commerce.

It's been three weeks. I sit with my friends, which is nice. But in accounts class, I doodle cells in the margins.

I think I chose my friends, not the subject. Can we talk on the phone this weekend? I don't know if it's too late to change.

Trisha

qa.a: All five of my friends ticked commerce.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling while sitting with the form?
qa.a: Trisha felt anxious, with a tight stomach, at the thought of walking into a class alone and standing out.

qa.q: What could Trisha do now, and who could help?
qa.a: Trisha could talk with Nazia didi and the school counsellor about whether switching to biology is still possible, and what it would take.

qa.a: The friends might be surprised or a bit sad at first, but real friends would likely stay close outside class.

You asked about the hair thing last year, Ujjwal? Okay. I'm Wasim. Let me tell you.

In Class 9, almost every boy in our section got the same haircut. Shaved at the sides, long on top. It started with two boys, then ten, then everyone.

I didn't like it. My face looked weird with it. But every day at lunch someone asked, "When are you getting it?" And when I said maybe never, they laughed.

I lay awake worrying about being the only one. It sounds silly now. But it felt huge.

So I got it. Abbu stared at me. My sister laughed so hard she cried.

The worst part was I still didn't like it. I kept touching the sides.

By the next term, half the boys had grown it out. Nobody even remembered.

I don't regret the haircut much. I regret that I couldn't just say, "Not for me."

qa.a: Shaved at the sides, long on top.

qa.q: Why did Wasim get the haircut even without liking it?
qa.a: Wasim felt anxious about being the only one without it and lay awake worrying, so fitting in felt more important than liking it.

qa.q: What could Wasim do the next time a trend comes along?
qa.a: Wasim could pause and ask whether the trend is liked or just feared missing, and practise saying "Not for me" calmly.

qa.q: How might Wasim's sister have seen the haircut?
qa.a: Wasim's sister found it very funny, laughing so hard she cried.

grounding: A teenager gets the haircut the whole class has, though it isn't liked, because standing out feels too risky.

Monday. The class group chat buzzed: "Mass bunk tomorrow after lunch! Everyone's in!" Ankita wasn't sure. She had a history test on Wednesday and liked that teacher. But forty-two people had replied "in". She typed "in" too, her stomach fluttering.

Tuesday. After lunch, the whole class walked out to the chai shop. Ankita went along, laughing with everyone, but she kept checking the time. Tenzin, her bench-mate, stayed behind. "I just don't want to," he'd said simply.

Friday. The principal called the whole class in. Everyone got a warning note for their parents. The history teacher looked disappointed. Tenzin, alone, got nothing.

On the way home, Ankita asked him, "Weren't you scared? Being the only one?"

"A bit," he admitted. "But I asked myself if I actually wanted to go. I didn't."

Ankita folded the warning note. She hadn't wanted to either. She had just wanted not to be the only one.

qa.a: Ankita felt anxious and unsure, her stomach fluttering, but afraid of being the only one who didn't join.

Wednesday

Joined the Entrepreneurship Cell today. Everyone's joining it. It had the longest queue at the club fair, like two hundred people. I figured if that many people want it, it must be the best club.

I didn't even stop at the music society's stall. That's the one I actually wanted. I've played guitar since I was twelve.

But Vaibhav said, "E-Cell is where everyone is. That's where the networking happens." And the queue was so long it felt like proof.

Now I'm lying here thinking. Two hundred people joining something doesn't mean it's right for me. It just means it's popular. And maybe half of them joined for the same reason I did: because the queue was long.

The music society had fifteen people. Fifteen people who actually love music.

Going back tomorrow to sign up there too. Maybe instead.

Nilesh

That June, every farmer in Jatin's village near Latur was sowing soybean. The seed shop had a queue down the road. Jatin, twenty-one and newly in charge of his father's fields, joined the queue too.

"Why soybean?" asked his sister Irawati, walking with him.

"Everyone's doing it."

"Last year you said the lower field floods. Soybean hates standing water."

"But the whole village can't be wrong."

"The whole village doesn't farm that field," Irawati said.

Jatin stopped. He had been so sure. Every neighbour, every uncle, every chat at the tea stall said soybean. It had felt like evidence.

But none of them had looked at his lower field.

He stepped out of the queue. "I'll ask the agriculture officer about the lower field first," he said. "Maybe soybean for the top field, something else below."

Irawati smiled. "Now you're farming, not following."

qa.q: What crop was every farmer sowing?
qa.a: Soybean.

qa.q: Why was Jatin going to sow soybean on all his fields?
qa.a: Jatin felt reassured because the whole village was doing it, and popularity felt like proof it was right.

qa.q: What did Jatin decide after Irawati's question, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Jatin decided to ask the agriculture officer about the lower field first, judging his own land rather than following the crowd.

qa.q: How does Irawati seem to see Jatin's final decision?
qa.a: Irawati seems pleased and proud, saying he's now farming rather than following.

Team lead's note, analytics team

Almost everyone in Tenzin's joining batch has applied for MBA programmes this year. It's become the thing to do: the lunch table talks of little else.

Tenzin came to me last week, unsure. She had the forms half filled. I asked her a simple question: "Why do you want it?"

She thought, then said, "Honestly, because everyone else is." Then she asked herself, out loud, "If nobody knew what I chose, would I still apply?"

She was quiet for a while. Then she said, "No. I'd do a data science certification. That's what I'm actually excited about."

She didn't mock her friends' choice. She said the MBA is right for some of them. She just decided, deliberately, that it wasn't right for her this year.

She submitted her certification application yesterday. She seemed calm, even happy.

Vinita

qa.q: How did Tenzin seem to feel after deciding?
qa.a: Tenzin seemed calm and even happy, having chosen deliberately rather than following the crowd.

qa.a: Asking why she wanted it and what she'd choose if nobody knew separated her real wish from the pull of the group.

qa.a: Her friends might be surprised at first, but since she didn't mock their choice, they're likely to respect it.

Monday night

Everyone in the office is running the city half marathon in December. There's a group chat, matching T-shirts, 6 a.m. practice runs. Bhavna asked me again today if I'm in.

My first instinct was yes, just because everyone is. Then I stopped and asked myself properly: why do I want this? And if nobody at work ever knew, would I still do it?

I thought about it on the bus.

The honest answer surprised me. Yes. I've wanted to try a long run since college. I was just scared I'd be the slowest. The crowd isn't the reason. It's the push.

So I told Bhavna yes, for my own reasons. I'll run at my pace, not theirs. If I'm last, fine.

It feels different to join when you've decided, instead of just being carried along.

Shalini

My name is Keerthana. During Onam, our teacher, Sharmila Miss, told the class that bats are birds. "They have wings and they fly," she said.

I had just read a book from the library that said bats are mammals. I was sure.

But Miss is always right. I wanted to raise my hand. I didn't.

At home, I told Amma. She said, "Why didn't you ask?" I said I was scared. It felt rude, like saying Miss was wrong.

Amma said, "You can respect someone and still ask a question. Say, 'Miss, my book says this. Can you help me understand?'"

The next day I did. Miss looked at the book, smiled and said, "You're right, Keerthana. Thank you."

I was so relieved.

qa.a: Bats are mammals.

qa.a: Amma said you can respect someone and still ask, and suggested a polite way: "My book says this. Can you help me understand?"

Class teacher's note, Class 3, December

Today, while decorating the class for Christmas, I wrote "7 × 8 = 54" on the board by mistake. Nobody said anything.

Later, I noticed Ganga's notebook. She had written 56, crossed it out, and written 54. When I asked why, she whispered, "You wrote 54, Miss. So I thought I was wrong."

She'd checked with counting on her fingers. But she said she was scared to tell me I made a mistake.

I realised my students trust me so much that they doubt their own correct answers.

Tomorrow I'll make one deliberate mistake on the board and give a star to whoever catches it. I want them to learn that questioning a teacher politely is good.

Yamini

qa.a: Ganga felt afraid and doubted herself, because trusting the teacher felt more important than trusting her own finger-counting.

qa.q: What does Yamini plan, and why is it a good idea?
qa.a: Yamini plans to make a deliberate mistake and reward whoever catches it, teaching children that polite questioning is welcome.

qa.q: How might the other children react to the deliberate-mistake game?
qa.a: The other children may feel surprised and excited, and braver about checking what is on the board.

The district match was the next morning, and training ran late in the heat. Coach Farida blew her whistle. "No water breaks today. Real athletes train through thirst. It makes you tough."

Vikas's head was pounding. He knew from science class that the body needs water in heat. His cousin, a nurse, had said the same.

But Coach Farida had played for the state. Everyone said she knew everything. And she sounded so sure.

He looked at his bottle on the bench. If he drank, would he look weak? Would she drop him?

After fifteen more minutes he felt dizzy. He walked to the bench, drank, and said, awkwardly, "Sorry, Coach. My cousin's a nurse. She says we need water in the heat."

The team went silent. Farida frowned. Then, slowly, she said, "Everyone, water. Two minutes."

Vikas's face burned. But his head started to clear.

qa.a: Coach Farida had played for the state.

qa.q: Why did Vikas hesitate to drink water?
qa.a: Vikas felt afraid of looking weak and being dropped, because the coach seemed so sure and had played for the state.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that was wise, even if awkward?
qa.a: Vikas drank water and politely mentioned his cousin's advice, looking after his health while respecting the coach.

qa.q: How might Coach Farida have felt when Vikas spoke up?
qa.a: Coach Farida may have felt surprised and a little challenged, but her call for a water break suggests she reconsidered.

Nilesh's mother, Tanuja, burst into his room. "Your exams are cancelled! It's in the family group. From the education minister himself."

Nilesh looked at the forwarded message. Bold letters, the state emblem, lots of exclamation marks.

His mother sounded so sure. She was a school principal. And the message looked official.

But something felt off. The date was wrong. There were spelling mistakes.

He hesitated. Correcting Ma felt awkward. She'd been right about so many things.

He checked. No announcement. Then the board's official page had a note: "Fake message circulating. Exams as scheduled."

He showed her. She read it, went a little red, and laughed. "I believed it because it looked official."

"I almost believed it because you believed it," Nilesh said.

They both laughed, a bit awkwardly.

Sudha had been a trainee at the electrical repair shop in Karad for three weeks. Madhav, the senior electrician, was respected by everyone in town.

On Tuesday, a streetlight needed fixing. Madhav said, "Climb up. No need for the harness, it takes too long. I never use it."

Sudha hesitated. The training manual said always use the harness. But Madhav had twenty years' experience. Saying no felt like calling him wrong, in front of the shop boy.

She climbed without it.

Halfway up, her foot slipped on the wet rung. She grabbed the pole and hung there, heart hammering. She climbed down slowly.

That evening, shaking, she told the shop owner what happened. He was quiet for a long moment. "The harness rule is for everyone. Even Madhav. I'll speak to him tomorrow."

Sudha realised she had known it was unsafe. She just couldn't find a polite way to say so.

qa.a: Sudha felt respect and nervousness toward Madhav, and saying no felt disrespectful, so she followed the unsafe instruction.

qa.q: What could Sudha say next time to object politely?
qa.a: Sudha could say, "Sir, the manual says harness always. I'll take two minutes to put it on," which respects him and stays safe.

qa.a: The owner was probably shocked and worried, and determined to enforce the harness rule for everyone.

In the hotel kitchen, Tarun was the youngest trainee cook. Eshaan was the sous-chef, famous for his temper and his skill.

On Saturday night, the restaurant was packed. Eshaan pointed at a tub of cream in the fridge. "Use that for the soup."

You asked about the conference, Nikita? Okay. I'm Bhupen, and I did something I was terrified to do.

The keynote speaker was a famous professor. I'd read all his books. During his talk, he said that remote teams "always" perform worse than office teams.

My own research showed the opposite for software teams. I'd spent two years on it.

At question time, my hands were sweating. I stood up and said, "Professor, thank you. I've admired your work for years. Could you tell us how you reached that conclusion? My study of 300 software teams found remote teams did slightly better."

The room went quiet. He paused. Then he said, "That's interesting. My data was mostly from manufacturing firms. It might not apply to software."

After the talk, he asked for my paper.

I think the trick was separating respect for him from agreeing with him.

I'm Lakshmi. I sat in on the budget meeting last week when Hemant, one of our analysts, did something I'd never seen anyone do with our director.

The director had said, very confidently, that "digital ads never work for our older customers". Everyone nodded. The director has been here twenty years.

Hemant raised his hand. "Sir, may I ask how we know that?"

The director looked surprised. "Experience."

Hemant nodded. "That makes sense. I only ask because last quarter we ran a small test with older customers. The response was better than print." He handed over a single printed chart. "I may be missing something. I'd really value your thoughts."

The director studied the chart for a long time. "Interesting. Let's run a bigger test."

I don't know what Hemant felt inside. But his voice stayed calm and polite the whole time. He respected the director. He just didn't pretend to agree.

qa.a: Lakshmi felt surprised and impressed, having never seen anyone question the director that way.

qa.a: Hemant asked how the claim was known, offered a single clear piece of evidence, admitted he might be missing something and stayed polite.

qa.a: The director was surprised at first, then seemed curious enough to approve a bigger test.

Amandeep had been head of the hospital's admin department for six months. In every weekly meeting, he'd share a plan, and everyone would nod. No questions. No objections.

At first he thought the plans were good. Then a new billing process he'd pushed failed badly. Afterwards, Anand, one of the clerks, admitted quietly, "We all thought it wouldn't work, sir. Nobody wanted to say."

Amandeep felt a chill. His title was silencing people.

At the next meeting, he tried something new. Before sharing his own view, he asked, "What problems do you see with this idea? I want to hear them first."

Silence. Then Anand spoke, carefully. Then two others.

After the meeting, Amandeep found Anand. "Thank you for speaking up. That's exactly what I need."

Over the next month, he thanked people publicly whenever they brought bad news early. The meetings got louder. And the plans got better.

qa.q: How long had Amandeep been head of the admin department?
qa.a: For six months.

qa.q: What did Amandeep feel when Anand admitted nobody wanted to speak?
qa.a: Amandeep felt a chill of alarm and some shame, realising his title was silencing his staff.

qa.q: What changes did Amandeep make, and why did they work?
qa.a: He asked for problems before sharing his view and thanked people who brought bad news, making disagreement feel safe.

qa.q: How might Anand have felt speaking first at the next meeting?
qa.a: Anand probably felt nervous but encouraged, since Amandeep had invited problems first.

grounding: A department head notices staff never disagree, realises his title mutes them and invites dissent early.

Santosh

You asked what surprised me most about being a manager, Sarita? I'm Pranav. I'll tell you.

When I got promoted last year, I thought I'd run great meetings. I'd present an idea, everyone would nod, we'd move on. I loved it.

Then a project went wrong. A big one. And after it failed, three people came to me separately and said they'd seen the problem coming months ago.

I asked, "Why didn't you say?"

One said, "You're the manager. We didn't want to seem rude."

That hurt. I realised the nodding wasn't agreement. It was my title shutting people up.

So I changed things. Now I ask for objections before I share my view. I say, "Tell me why this won't work." And when someone brings bad news, I thank them in front of everyone.

At first it was awkward. Now people argue with me all the time. The work is much better.

qa.a: Three people came to me separately.

qa.a: Pranav felt hurt, realising the nodding came from fear of the title, not agreement.

qa.q: What did Pranav change, and why did it help?
qa.a: Pranav asked for objections before sharing a personal view and thanked bad news publicly, which made dissent safe and improved the work.

qa.q: How might Pranav's team feel now?
qa.a: The team probably feels freer and more valued, since their objections are welcomed.

grounding: A new manager notices staff never disagree, realises the title mutes them and invites dissent early.

Usha, you're angry at the other house for cheating in kho-kho? Hmm. Sit. Let your Karthik thatha tell you about Pongal sports day when I was ten.

Being Green felt so good that I stopped seeing fairly.
